analysis.one_liner: Creates a declining national cap on greenhouse gas emissions with tradable pollution allowances and funds for consumers and workers.
analysis.headline: The Senate voted 74–14 in June 2008 just to begin debating the bill, but it was returned to the calendar in July 2008 and never received a vote on passage before the Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required factories, power plants, refineries, and fuel producers to hold an allowance for every ton of greenhouse gases they emit, with the number of allowances shrinking each year through 2050. Companies could trade, bank, borrow, or buy offsets in place of allowances. Part of the money from auctioning allowances would have gone to low-income energy consumers, worker retraining, clean-energy technology, and assistance to states. The Senate voted 74–14 just to start debating it, but the bill never received a vote on passage and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people would benefit from cleaner air and a slower pace of climate change, since the declining cap targeted the pollution from coal, oil, and gas that drives warming and health harms. Low- and middle-income households were specifically protected: states had to use allowances to mitigate impacts on low-income energy consumers, and an Energy Assistance Fund funded from auction proceeds would help pay energy bills. Workers in fossil fuel-dependent industries would get retraining money, and new clean-energy industries would gain guaranteed demand. Farmers and foresters could earn new revenue selling carbon offsets.

how_it_helps.text: Set a hard, declining cap on total US greenhouse gas emissions from 2012 through 2050, starting at about 5.8 billion tons in 2012 and falling to about 1.7 billion tons by 2050.

Directed auction proceeds to an Energy Assistance Fund and required states to use allocated allowances to mitigate impacts on low-income energy consumers, so the households most exposed to higher energy bills would get help.
Funded a Climate Change Worker Training Program to retrain workers whose jobs depend on fossil fuels, plus funds for adaptation and emergency firefighting.

Created a Carbon Market Efficiency Board empowered to implement cost relief if the emission market posed significant harm to the economy, and allowed borrowing of future allowances and a domestic offset program to contain compliance costs.

Required an international reserve allowance program aimed at pushing foreign countries to address their own emissions, and established an international adaptation program for disadvantaged communities abroad.

analysis.who_pays: The covered industries — coal-using facilities, natural gas processors, petroleum refiners and importers, and chemical producers — would bear the cost of buying allowances or reducing emissions, and much of that cost would be passed to consumers through higher prices for electricity, gasoline, and heating fuel, which is why the bill built in cost relief and low-income assistance.
analysis.who_pays_short: Fossil fuel producers and energy users

drawbacks.text: Rather than auction all allowances, the bill gave a substantial share free to the fossil fuel companies and energy-intensive manufacturers it regulated, including allocations to coal-fired power plants, petroleum refiners, and HFC producers — meaning polluters would have been compensated for a cost they had long imposed on the public without charge.

A cap-and-trade system allows companies to buy and sell the right to pollute, creating a new financial market in emission permits; the bill even provided for banking, borrowing, and unrestricted trading of allowances [S3], which critics warned could enrich financial intermediaries and let polluters delay real cuts by purchasing cheap allowances and offsets.

Companies could satisfy up to 15% of their obligation with offsets — reductions claimed outside the capped sectors — and could borrow future allowances with interest [S3], flexibility that weakens the certainty that the scheduled emission cuts actually happen on time.

Compliance costs on fuels and electricity would likely be passed to consumers as higher energy prices; the bill's own cost-relief mechanisms and Energy Assistance Fund acknowledge this burden on ordinary households.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would have delivered large long-term public benefits — a steadily declining cap on the pollution driving climate change, funded protections for low-income energy consumers, and new clean-energy industries — but it carried real costs and design compromises: energy prices would have risen for households in the near term, and to win industry acquiescence it gave away a large share of allowances to fossil fuel utilities and manufacturers, auctioning only part of them and in effect compensating polluters for a duty they had previously imposed on the public for free. Its offset and borrowing provisions also risked slowing real reductions. On balance it was a serious, if imperfect, attempt to address a threat the bill's own findings describe as endangering public health and national security [S3]; letting it fail meant those benefits were deferred indefinitely.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate voted 74–14 just to open debate in June 2008, but the bill was returned to the calendar in July and never came up for an up-or-down vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: After Boxer introduced the bill on May 20, 2008, Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid moved to bring it to the floor; that motion initially stalled, and a cloture motion (a vote to end delay tactics) was filed on the motion to proceed on May 22, 2008 [S5].

On June 2, 2008, the Senate invoked cloture on the motion to proceed 74–14, with 40 of 49 voting Democrats and 32 of 49 voting Republicans in favor — a strong bipartisan showing merely to begin debating the bill [S6].

The Senate debated the bill in early June 2008, including a motion by Senator Reid to commit it back to the Environment and Public Works Committee with instructions, but the chamber never voted on the bill itself [S5].
On July 8, 2008, the bill was returned to the Senate calendar, where it stayed until the 110th Congress ended in January 2009 without passage [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The fossil fuel industries and energy-intensive manufacturers the bill would have capped came out ahead, since they avoided compliance costs and the loss of free allowance value; ordinary consumers avoided possible near-term energy price increases but lost the chance at a national climate program.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Fossil fuel interests the bill would have capped

for.name: Sen. Barbara Boxer
for.role: Chair, Senate Environment and Public Works Committee; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced S. 3036 in the Senate and led its floor consideration.

for.name: 74 senators
for.what_they_did: Voted 74–14 to invoke cloture on the motion to proceed, clearing the way for the Senate to debate the bill.

for.name: Environmental and climate advocacy groups
for.what_they_did: Publicly backed the bill as the most serious congressional climate legislation to date.

against.name: Fossil fuel and manufacturing industry lobbies
against.role: Coal, oil, electric utility, and manufacturing interests
against.what_they_did: Fiercely opposed the bill as a costly energy tax; their public campaign against cap-and-trade helped deny the bill the votes to reach passage.

against.name: President George W. Bush
against.what_they_did: Opposed the bill and threatened a veto, removing any incentive for Senate opponents to support it.

against.name: Senate Republicans and conservative Democrats
against.what_they_did: Forced the full 491-page bill to be read into the record and demanded the CBO's cost estimate, slowing the floor process; a bloc of 13 voting Republicans and one Democrat voted against even opening debate [S6].

sides.party_line_note: The only recorded vote, the 74–14 cloture vote to begin debate, was bipartisan: 40 of 49 voting Democrats and 32 of 49 voting Republicans voted yes, while 13 Republicans and one Democrat voted no [S6].

industries.industry: Coal producers and coal-fired power plants
industries.note: Coal combustion would have required emission allowances under a shrinking cap, directly threatening coal demand and coal plant economics, though the bill also gave free allowances and advanced-coal funding to cushion the sector. Its defeat preserved coal's existing position.

Utilities faced compliance costs under the cap but would have received transition allowances for fossil-fired plants and rural cooperatives, plus money for zero- and low-carbon technology; the public would bear much of the pass-through in rates.

industries.industry: Oil refiners and petroleum fuel producers/importers
industries.note: Refiners and importers of petroleum-based fuels would have had to surrender allowances for the emissions from every gallon sold, a cost likely passed to drivers at the pump.
Gas processors, producers, and importers would have been covered entities facing allowance costs, though natural gas generally benefits over coal under any carbon cap.
A declining cap with auction proceeds for zero- or low-carbon energy, cellulosic biomass fuel, and advanced vehicle manufacturing would have created guaranteed demand for clean-energy technology.

The bill created a domestic offset program letting farmers, foresters, and landowners earn new revenue for sequestration projects, and even mandated an outreach program to teach producers how to profit from it.
Emission allowances would have been freely tradable by anyone, creating a large new commodity market for brokers and traders; critics of cap-and-trade worry about speculation in a public resource.
